classification.difficultyReason: Translate equal compass radii into four equal sides, then apply the appropriate rhombus diagonal property. Each construction explicitly supplies the rhombus intermediate step, making these routine linked deductions.

content.prompt: This question justifies some of the constructions that you learnt in earlier years.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The diagram shows the standard construction of the perpendicular bisector of a given interval $AB$. We draw two arcs with centres $A$ and $B$ respectively, equal radius, intersecting at $P$ and $Q$.

spec.description: Equal-radius compass arcs intersect above and below AB. The constructed bisector remains dashed red; ordinary arcs, interval, point markers and labels use black. Rhombus sides are not added.
spec.mathematics: AP=AQ=BP=BQ; P and Q are the two circle intersections.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied construction is visible; no right-angle mark or rhombus sides are added.

answer.short: $AP=AQ=BP=BQ$, since all are radii of the equal-radius arcs. Thus $APBQ$ has four equal sides.
answer.worked: $AP=AQ$ and $BP=BQ$ are radii of their respective arcs. Both arcs have the same radius, so $AP=PB=BQ=QA$. Hence $APBQ$ is a rhombus.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence explain why $PQ$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

answer.short: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, so $PQ$ perpendicularly bisects $AB$.
answer.worked: $AB$ and $PQ$ are the diagonals of rhombus $APBQ$. Its diagonals bisect each other at right angles. Therefore $PQ$ passes through the midpoint of $AB$ and is perpendicular to $AB$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: The diagram shows the standard construction of the bisector of a given angle $\angle AOB$. We draw three arcs with centres $O$, $P$ and $Q$ respectively, and equal radius.

spec.description: Angle AOB with all three equal-radius construction arcs and the dashed red constructed ray OM. The illustrative opening has no numerical angle label. Ordinary strokes and point markers use black.
spec.mathematics: P lies on OA and Q on OB; OP=OQ=PM=QM. M is the interior intersection of the arcs centred at P and Q.
spec.answerVisibility: No equal-angle marks or rhombus edges are added.

answer.short: $OP=OQ=PM=QM$, since the three arcs have equal radius. Thus $OPMQ$ has four equal sides.
answer.worked: $OP$ and $OQ$ are radii of the arc centred at $O$; $PM$ and $QM$ are radii of the arcs centred at $P$ and $Q$. All three radii are equal, so $OP=PM=MQ=QO$. Therefore $OPMQ$ is a rhombus.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence explain why $OM$ is the bisector of $\angle AOB$.

answer.short: A rhombus diagonal bisects the vertex angles through which it passes. Hence $OM$ bisects $\angle POQ=\angle AOB$.
answer.worked: $OM$ is a diagonal of rhombus $OPMQ$, so it bisects $\angle POQ$. Since $P$ lies on ray $OA$ and $Q$ lies on ray $OB$, $\angle POQ=\angle AOB$. Hence $OM$ bisects $\angle AOB$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The diagram shows the standard construction of the perpendicular from a given point $P$ to a given line $\ell$. First draw an arc with centre $P$ cutting $\ell$ at $A$ and $B$. Then with centres $A$ and $B$ and the same radius, draw arcs meeting at $M$.

spec.description: Line ell through A and B; P above and M below. Retains the arc centred at P and two separate arcs centred at A and B. The constructed perpendicular remains dashed red; ordinary strokes and point markers use black.
spec.mathematics: PA=PB=AM=BM, using the same radius for all three arcs. PM is the line through the two equal-radius circle intersections P and M.
spec.answerVisibility: No right-angle mark or rhombus sides are added.

answer.short: $PA=PB=AM=BM$, since all three arcs use the same radius. Thus $APBM$ has four equal sides.
answer.worked: $PA=PB$ are radii of the first arc. The arcs centred at $A$ and $B$ use this same radius, so $AM=BM=PA=PB$. Hence $APBM$ is a rhombus.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Hence explain why $PM$ is perpendicular to $\ell$.

answer.short: The rhombus diagonals $PM$ and $AB$ meet at right angles. Since $AB$ lies on $\ell$, $PM\perp\ell$.
answer.worked: $PM$ and $AB$ are the diagonals of rhombus $APBM$, so $PM\perp AB$. Since $A$ and $B$ lie on $\ell$, it follows that $PM\perp\ell$.
